passage: In his Oslo classroom, Lars noticed that Pablo, nine, had not raised his hand once all term. During the fractions discussion he stared at his desk while others shouted answers. Lars had begun to wonder if Pablo was bored. Then he read the maths journals. Pablo had written a full page: how to share three pizzas among eight friends fairly, with drawings and a joke about the crust. It was the best answer in the class. The next week, Lars put a "question box" on his desk for written ideas, and spent two minutes with Pablo each Friday. "Tell me one thing you noticed this week." Pablo spoke quietly, but for longer every time.

qa.q: How many pizzas did Pablo write about sharing?
qa.a: Three pizzas among eight friends.

qa.q: How did Lars feel after reading Pablo's journal?
qa.a: He felt surprised and impressed, realising Pablo's silence was not boredom.

qa.q: What did Lars do to let Pablo show what he knows?
qa.a: He set up a question box for written ideas and short one-to-one chats each Friday.

qa.q: How might Pablo feel during the Friday chats?
qa.a: Pablo may feel safe and valued, which is why he speaks a little longer each time.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a silent pupil who writes thoughtful answers, realising silence isn't disinterest and offering written and one-to-one routes.

passage:
"Nazia, you're going to Kabir's farmhouse party tonight? After the fair and the movie?"
"Obviously, Reena. Everyone's going."
"You've said yes to every plan this month. Are you even tired?"
"Tired is better than sitting at home. When I'm alone I feel flat, like switched off."
"Okay. But how are you getting there?"
"Arjun's driving. He just got his licence."
"The one who raced his bike at the flyover?"
Nazia paused. "Everyone's going with him."
"So would you go if nobody asked you?"
A long silence. "Maybe not with Arjun."
"Come to mine instead. Movie night. My cousins are coming, it'll be loud."
Nazia laughed. "Loud is good. Okay. I'll text them I'm not coming."

qa.q: Who was going to drive to the farmhouse party?
qa.a: Arjun, who just got his licence.

qa.q: How does Nazia feel when she is alone?
qa.a: Nazia feels flat, as if switched off.

qa.q: How did Reena help Nazia avoid a risky choice?
qa.a: She asked whether Nazia really wanted to go, pointed out the risky driver and offered a loud gathering at home instead.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Nazia agrees to come over?
qa.a: Reena may feel relieved and glad, knowing Nazia chose company without the risk.

grounding: Shows a teenager who feels most alive in company and says yes to every plan, with a friend showing where peer-pleasing could slide into risk.

passage: In Prague, Tomas, fifteen, came home from school every day, said "Ahoj" to his mother and shut his door. Guitar, headphones, silence. In class he spoke rarely, thinking long before answering, and group presentations left him wiped out for the evening. Some classmates called him arrogant. Fatima, his friend since they were eight, knew better. On Saturday he played her a song he'd written, slow and careful, about her grandmother's hospital stay last winter. She hadn't known he'd noticed how scared she'd been. Fatima wiped her eyes. "You remember everything." Tomas shrugged, embarrassed. "I just listen." On Monday, when a boy mocked her accent, Tomas was the one who quietly stood beside her.

qa.q: What did Tomas's song describe?
qa.a: Fatima's grandmother's hospital stay last winter.

qa.q: How does Tomas feel after group presentations?
qa.a: He feels tired and wiped out for the evening, needing quiet to recharge.

qa.q: What does the song show that classmates miss about Tomas?
qa.a: It shows his deep thoughtfulness and loyalty, which classmates mistake for arrogance.

qa.q: How did Fatima feel when she heard the song?
qa.a: She felt moved and understood, wiping her eyes because Tomas had noticed her fear.

grounding: Shows a teenager who recharges alone, thinks before speaking and tires of group work, mistaken for aloof but deep-thinking and loyal to a friend.

passage:
Saturday: The group went to the arcade again, then karaoke. Joseph, fifteen, looked grey by eight. When the others chanted, "Joseph, sing!" he shook his head. Somebody pulled him up anyway. He mumbled one line and left early.
Monday: Sachin caught Joseph at the bus stop. "Saturday was too much, right? How much hanging out do you actually want?" Joseph thought. "One loud thing a week is fun. More than that and I'm wrecked." Sachin nodded. "And Rohit feels left out when we skip plans. Let's mix it up."
The next Saturday: They played board games on Sachin's terrace, six of them, snacks and slow jokes. Nobody asked Joseph to perform. He laughed more than anyone. The Saturday after, the arcade again, and Joseph came.

qa.q: Where did the group play board games?
qa.a: On Sachin's terrace.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel by the end of the karaoke night?
qa.a: He felt drained and exhausted, looking grey and leaving early after being pulled up to sing.

qa.q: What did Sachin do that respected both energies in the group?
qa.a: He asked Joseph how much company he wanted and helped the group mix loud outings with quiet ones, without pushing anyone to perform.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel seeing Joseph laugh on the terrace?
qa.a: Sachin likely feels pleased and relieved that simply asking about Joseph's needs made the group better for everyone.

grounding: Shows a friend group that plans both loud and quiet outings, stops pushing a tired friend to perform and asks how much company each wants.

passage:
Thursday, 11 p.m.
Startup meetup at the college today. I pitched our app to four investors, answered every question, laughed at the right jokes. Dhruv said I was "a natural." Inside I was running on fumes.
After, everyone went to the after-party. I went back to my room, turned off the lights and lay on the floor for two hours. I felt guilty. Wasn't I supposed to network?
But then I remembered what worked last time. I didn't need fifty conversations. Today I had three good ones: the investor who asked about our users, the founder from Pune, the girl who builds drones. I've saved their numbers.
Dhruv just texted: "Where are you?" I wrote back, "Recharging. Coffee tomorrow?" No guilt. Well, almost none.
Sumit

qa.q: How many investors did Sumit pitch to?
qa.a: Four investors.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel about skipping the after-party?
qa.a: Sumit felt guilty at first, wondering if skipping networking was wrong, then mostly at peace.

qa.q: What did Sumit learn about handling networking events?
qa.a: To focus on a few meaningful conversations and say no to the rest without guilt, taking time alone to recharge.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Sumit after the meetup?
qa.a: Dhruv sees Sumit as a natural performer, perhaps not realising how much energy it took.

grounding: Shows a young adult who performs well at a networking event but needs hours alone, learning to choose a few meaningful conversations and skip the rest without guilt.

passage:
Manager's note, Supply Team, Q3. Written by Damini.
Kishore, twenty-five, has been on the team for eight months. In our Monday meetings he rarely speaks while louder voices fill the room, and at first I assumed he had little to add. Then in July he sent a two-page email explaining why our deliveries to the eastern warehouses were always late, with a simple fix. It was brilliant. It had also been ignored for a week because nobody reads long emails after a meeting.
Since then I've changed two things. I send the agenda a day early and ask for written input beforehand. And I ask Kishore by name, "What did you notice?" He speaks for two clear minutes. The eastern deliveries are now on time.

qa.q: What problem did Kishore's email explain?
qa.a: Why deliveries to the eastern warehouses were always late.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel when Damini asks him by name?
qa.a: He likely feels valued and more comfortable, able to share clearly for two minutes.

qa.q: What changes helped Kishore's ideas get heard?
qa.a: Sending the agenda early for written input and asking him directly for his observations in meetings.

qa.q: How did Damini first see Kishore, and how did that change?
qa.a: Damini first assumed he had little to add, then recognised his careful thinking after the email.

grounding: Shows a quiet young professional who shares best in writing, whose ideas are overlooked until his manager creates small openings and asks for his input.

passage: At the playgroup in Bergen, Ingrid, two, saw Esther crying by the swings. She toddled over, patted Esther's arm and held out her own rice cake. When the teacher said, "Tidy-up time!" Ingrid happily carried the blocks. But the teacher noticed Ingrid always let others take the swing first. She knelt. "Ingrid, do you want a turn too?" Ingrid looked at the swing, then nodded hard.

qa.q: What did Ingrid offer Esther?
qa.a: Her own rice cake.

qa.q: What does Ingrid's nod suggest about her wants?
qa.a: It suggests she really wanted a turn on the swing but was too eager to please to ask.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that was wise?
qa.a: The teacher noticed Ingrid always gave way and gently asked about her own wish.

qa.q: How might Esther have felt when Ingrid patted her arm?
qa.a: Esther may have felt comforted and less alone.

grounding: Shows a toddler who comforts a peer, shares and follows requests happily, and an adult asking about the unspoken wants her warmth can hide.

passage: At the village well, Bhavna, six, marched up to a big boy who had pushed his bucket ahead of hers. "You pushed in! That's not fair. I was here first." The boy blinked and stepped back. At lunch she told her grandmother, Vandana, "Your roti is burnt on this side." Vandana laughed. "You're right. But how could you say it so I'd feel nice?" Bhavna frowned, thinking hard. "Dadi, this side is a little burnt, but the other side is yummy?" "Much better." Bhavna nodded, satisfied, and ate the good side first.

qa.q: What did the big boy do at the well?
qa.a: He pushed his bucket ahead of Bhavna's.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when the boy pushed in?
qa.a: She felt angry at the unfairness and determined to stand up for herself.

qa.q: How did Vandana guide Bhavna?
qa.a: She agreed Bhavna was right but helped her find a kinder way to say the same honest thing.

qa.q: How might the big boy have felt when Bhavna challenged him?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, stepping back.

grounding: Shows a blunt, determined child who argues for fairness and says what she thinks, and a grandmother guiding her toward kindness in tone.

passage:
Class note, Year 4, Friday. Written by Deepak.
Bhavna, nine, is loved by everyone. This week I saw why, and also what it costs her. At break she played "teacher" three days running, always as the scolded student, though I know she wanted to play hopscotch. On Wednesday, when a clay pot broke, she said, "It was me," though I'd seen another child knock it. She looked relieved once the fuss ended.
I spoke to her quietly after class. She said, "If everyone's happy, I feel safe." We practised a few sentences: "I want to play hopscotch today," and "I didn't break it." On Friday she tried the first one. Her friends switched games without a fuss. She came back beaming.

qa.q: What game did Bhavna want to play?
qa.a: Hopscotch.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel after taking the blame for the pot?
qa.a: She felt relieved once the fuss ended, because conflict made her feel unsafe.

qa.q: How did Deepak help Bhavna learn that saying no is safe?
qa.a: Deepak spoke with her privately and practised simple sentences to say what she wants and what is true.

qa.q: How did Bhavna's friends react when she said what she wanted?
qa.a: They switched games without any fuss, showing her the friendship was still safe.

grounding: Shows a people-pleasing child who agrees to disliked games and takes blame to avoid conflict, and a teacher helping her learn that saying no doesn't break friendship.

passage:
Wednesday
Told Mawii her song for the school contest was off-key in the second verse. It WAS. But she went quiet and walked off, and I felt bad all through maths. I always say the hard thing. Sometimes I should say it softer.
But then at lunch, the girls started laughing at the new girl's accent, and they looked at me to join in. I didn't. I said, "That's not funny." Nobody spoke to me for the rest of lunch. I don't care. Well, I care a bit.
And in PE I told Francis Sir straight out that picking the team captain by who's tallest isn't fair. He actually listened and said we'd vote next week.
Tonight I'll text Mawii sorry for how I said it. Not for what I said.
Lalremsiami

qa.q: What did Francis Sir agree to do next week?
qa.a: Let the class vote for the team captain.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after telling Mawii her song was off-key?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt bad all through maths, knowing the honest words hurt Mawii.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami's bluntness help in other moments?
qa.a: It lets Lalremsiami refuse to join the mocking and speak up about the unfair captain rule.

qa.q: How might Mawii feel after getting the apology text?
qa.a: Mawii may feel hurt still but soothed, understanding the feedback was honest, not cruel.

grounding: Shows a blunt teenager whose honesty can hurt a friend but who resists peer pressure and speaks up against unfairness, learning to soften the tone.
